reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Bolognia Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Presents with the abrupt onset of tender, red-to-violaceous plaques and nodules, often with fever and a raised neutrophil count
Lesions typically favour the face, neck, and upper limbs and may look oedematous or pseudovesicular ('juicy' plaques)
Histology shows a dense dermal infiltrate of neutrophils without evidence of true vasculitis

Recognised subtypes are classic or idiopathic (often post-infectious or associated with inflammatory bowel disease and pregnancy), malignancy-associated (notably acute myeloid leukaemia), and drug-induced
Drug-induced disease is classically linked to granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and several other medications
Pathergy may occur, with new lesions arising at sites of trauma, and extracutaneous neutrophilic involvement of eyes, joints, lungs, and other organs can accompany the skin disease
Responds briskly to systemic glucocorticoids, with steroid-sparing agents used for recurrent or refractory disease and treatment of any underlying trigger
reference.pathophysiology: Sweet syndrome is a reactive neutrophilic dermatosis in which activated neutrophils accumulate in the dermis, producing tender inflammatory plaques, fever, and systemic inflammation. It is thought to reflect a hypersensitivity-type response driven by cytokines and colony-stimulating factors that recruit and activate neutrophils, rather than by infection or primary vasculitis. Triggers include preceding infections, inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, pregnancy, certain drugs, and, importantly, underlying malignancy, most often myeloid haematological disorders, where the syndrome can be paraneoplastic. Dysregulated innate immune activation and possible clonal myeloid contributions underlie the neutrophil-rich inflammation.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing dense dermal neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis
Full blood count with differential for neutrophilia and to screen for haematological disease
Inflammatory markers such as ESR and CRP
Blood film and, where indicated, haematology referral to exclude myeloid malignancy
Review of recent medications, especially colony-stimulating factors
Investigations for associated infection, inflammatory bowel disease, or other trigger as guided by history
redFlags: Features suggesting underlying acute myeloid leukaemia or myelodysplasia such as cytopenias or abnormal blood film
Systemic neutrophilic involvement of lungs, eyes, or central nervous system
Recurrent or treatment-resistant disease prompting a search for occult malignancy
Severe systemic upset with high fever mimicking sepsis
reference.prognosis: Classic and drug-induced disease usually responds rapidly to glucocorticoids and often resolves, though recurrences occur; malignancy-associated disease tends to follow the course of the underlying cancer and may relapse with disease activity.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing tender plaques as cellulitis and treating with antibiotics alone
Failing to investigate for an underlying haematological malignancy, particularly in recurrent or atypical cases
Overlooking a recent drug, such as a colony-stimulating factor, as the cause
Not recognising extracutaneous neutrophilic organ involvement
management: Systemic corticosteroids are the mainstay and typically produce rapid resolution of skin lesions and systemic inflammation
Identify and remove or treat the trigger, withdrawing a culprit drug such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factor and treating associated infection or inflammatory bowel disease
Use steroid-sparing agents such as colchicine, dapsone or potassium iodide for recurrent, refractory or steroid-intolerant disease
Treat localised disease with potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids
Investigate for and manage an underlying malignancy, particularly acute myeloid leukaemia, since paraneoplastic disease tracks the cancer
Monitor for recurrence during corticosteroid tapering and with reactivation of any associated disease
Involve dermatology and, where malignancy is suspected, haematology in ongoing care
